name: Sursurunga
confidence_why: Hutchisson and Hutchisson's 1985 updated phonology, the only first-hand description of Sursurunga stress, states without hedging that primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable and expressly replaces the same authors' 1975 preliminary account, which had tentatively described a weight-driven system with final stress, so the penultimate reading has a clear winner but rests on a single fieldwork team.

catalog_locator: 1985 Updated Phonology, sec. 6.2 'Word Stress', pp.17-18 (pp.17-18); 1975 Preliminary Phonology sec. 6.2 p.186 (p.24) for the superseded statement
catalog_quote: 6.2 Word Stress. Word stress in Sursurunga is predictable and operates according to the following rules: 1. When all syllables in the word are identical in both CV pattern and phoneme quality, stress tends to be equal on all syllables. 2. In all other cases, primary stress occurs on the penultimate syllable with secondary stress on the alternate regressive syllables when they are present. Identical syllables: /'dik'dik'dik/ 'shaking', /'dok'dok/ 'fruit harvesting stick' ... 2-syllable words: /'guai/ 'to make wet', ... /'kalau/ 'male'. 3-syllable words: /gur'guran/ 'to wash clothes', /i'lilim/ 'to wash hands' ... 4-syllable words: /'alek'tadai/ 'to turn upside down', /'kalas'tari/ 'caught', /'kawa'liklik/ 'kinship group'. 5-syllable words: /u'tungti'mani/ 'to explain', /par'asak'saknai/ 'to relate untruthfully but not necessarily intentionally'.

new_statements.quote: Word stress has not yet been fully analyzed, but the following are some observations noted thus far. The basic stress system is determined by the vowel and consonant content and the CV patterns of the word. All factors being equal between all syllables in the word, a secondary stress law comes into effect: that primary stress falls on the last syllable, and that heavy secondary stress falls on the first syllable of two and three syllable words. Four and five syllable words do not seem to be affected by a secondary law. [p. 187:] Probably the strongest consonant is /r/. Normally, any syllable containing /r/ will receive stress.
new_statements.citation: Hutchisson, Sharon and Hutchisson, Don (1975). A preliminary phonology of Sursurunga. In Phonologies of five Austronesian languages. Workpapers in Papua New Guinea Languages 13. Ukarumpa: Summer Institute of Linguistics. pp. 163-202.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog rule (penultimate stress = penultimate primary) comes from the same authors' 1985 'An updated phonology of Sursurunga' (sec. 6.2, pp. 17-18, also held by the project and re-read today: 'primary stress occurs on the penultimate syllable with secondary stress on the alternate regressive syllables'). The 1975 preliminary statement differs in type and placement: segment/CV-pattern strength decides stress, and the equal-syllables default is FINAL primary + initial secondary, not penult. The disagreement is diachronic within one author pair: the 1985 typescript explicitly revises the 1974-75 preliminary after ten more years of fieldwork, so the 1975 statement is superseded rather than…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Explicitly preliminary ('not yet been fully analyzed'). Stress is attracted by 'strong' segments and syllable types: lower vowels and /u/ are strong, /i/ and /ə/ weak; /r/ is the strongest consonant and a syllable containing it normally takes stress; CVV and CVC syllables outrank other patterns. Only when all syllables are equal does a positional default apply: primary stress on the last syllable, with heavy secondary stress on the first syllable of two- and three-syllable words. Examples p. 187: /ˈru.pi/ 'to scrape', /ruˈrut/ 'to look for lice', /ˈkau.ra/ 'to set (as the sun)', /ˈgorˈsai/ 'to wash with water'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'heavy secondary stress falls on the first syllable of two and three syllable words. Four and five syllable words do not seem to be affected by a secondary law' (p. 186).
new_statements.exceptions: p. 187: 'Strong ones naturally receive heavier stress than weak ones. Lower vowels and /u/ are strong; /i/ and /ə/ are weak' (so /gaur/ 'you two' and /təil/ 'to precede' sound evenly stressed, /giur/ 'we two (excl.)' stressed on the second syllable); 'Exceptions [to /r/ attracting stress] are determined by other strong consonant and vowel combinations contiguous to the syllable containing /r/ and by surrounding CV patterns'; 'Some CV patterns such as CVV and CVC are stronger than others. When they are combined in words with other patterns, they receive the stress; when they are combined with themselves, stress tends to be equal.' Sec. 6.3 Intonation: 'Intonational contours convey grammatical meaning and may perturb stress.'
new_statements.identity_note: The 1975 paper (p. 163) describes the east-coast dialect of speakers 'who have always lived on the coast' (language teachers Tokialir Orim and Sam Tuaen, Tekedan village, Namatanai Subdistrict, New Ireland; fieldwork from 17 April 1974, seven months), as opposed to the dialect of formerly inland people resettled on the coast. The 1985 update covers the same language (approx. 2800 speakers, Namatanai Subprovince).

readall_conflicts: The only listed work (Hutchisson & Hutchisson 1975, sec. 6.2, p. 186-187) gives a weight-sensitive system with a final-stress default and initial secondary stress in 2-3 syllable words, hedged as 'not yet been fully analyzed'. The catalog's penultimate rule rests on the same authors' 1985 'An updated phonology of Sursurunga' (sec. 6.2, pp. 17-18, opened for context), which states unhedged that 'primary stress occurs on the penultimate syllable with secondary stress on the alternate regressive syllables', with equal stress only when all syllables are identical. The two descriptions therefore conflict (final/weight-driven vs. penult/weight-blind), but the later one explicitly supersedes the earlier by the same fieldworkers, so the catalog's penult reading stands; the 1975 statement should be recorded as the superseded preliminary view, not as an independent contradicting source.

audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation is verbatim at the stated locator (1985 Updated Phonology sec. 6.2, pp.17-18), verified from page scan since the PDF has no text. The source is the most recent and most specific stress description that exists for Sursurunga, written by the long-term fieldworkers and explicitly superseding their weight/segment-driven 1975 'not yet fully analyzed' account (which our record correctly notes as superseded and which explains the 31 Aug quick-screen 'weight-sensitive' misclassification). The later 2018 dictionary (held, checked) is silent on stress, so nothing newer contradicts penultimate primary + alternating leftward secondary. Coding 'fixed penult, weight-blind, listed exception for fully identical-syllable words' matches the source exactly. One minor caveat worth keeping in mind, not an action: the typescript marks primary and secondary stress with the same r
